sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A curve that rises and is cut off at a finite time.
sections.body_md:
A predictive controller writes a finite-horizon problem at the current state, solves it, and applies only the first input. At the next sample it throws the rest of the sequence away and starts again from the new state. That last habit is what makes the method closed loop. Applying the whole sequence would be an open-loop plan that never looks at another measurement.

The horizon can carry constraints. A bound on the command is a constraint, not a weight. The quadratic regulator is the different limit: infinite horizon, no constraint, and one constant gain.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
A one-step scalar illustration minimizes \((x+u)^2 + \rho u^2\). The derivative in \(u\) vanishes at
\[
u = -\frac{x}{1+\rho}.
\]
If the command must also lie in an interval, and the cost is convex, the constrained minimizer is that unconstrained value clipped to the interval. A longer horizon replaces this one square by a sum of predicted stage costs, with the model rolling the state forward, and the same rule applies to the implementation: keep the first input only.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take \(x = 5.61\) and \(\rho = 0.6\), with no constraint. The command is \(-5.61 / 1.6 = -3.50625\). A bound \(|u| \le 2.8\) would clip that command to \(-2.8\), because \(3.50625\) sits past the stop. The unconstrained number and the clipped number are different questions. Reporting \(5.61\) reports the state.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The sign of the one-step command is negative when \(x\) is positive and the predicted state is \(x+u\): you are pulling the state back. Clipping to the positive end of a symmetric interval doubles the error. Dividing by \(\rho\) alone drops the \(1\) that came from the state penalty. And a longer horizon is not free: the first input can change, because the plan now feels costs and constraints that used to sit past the end of the window.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: If the model is only trustworthy near one operating condition, a table of linear controllers indexed by a measurement is a different architecture from one horizon on a single model. If the cost is quadratic, the horizon infinite, and the constraints absent, the first input collapses to the constant regulator gain. Knowing which of those limits you are in is how you decide whether the extra optimization at each sample is doing any work.
